They say: "Could I find my proper groove, What a deep mark I would make!" So they chop and change, and each fresh move Is only a fresh mistake. And each forgets, as he strips and runs With a brilliant, fitful pace, It's the steady, quiet, plodding ones Who win in the lifelong race. He is one of the Legion Lost; He was never meant to win; He's a rolling stone, and it's bred in the bone; He's a man who won't fit in.

Here are a few ways to polish this text, depending on your desired tone and format. 

### Option 1: Elevated Eloquent Prose (Recommended)
*Best suited for speeches, reflective essays, or sophisticated literary contexts. It transforms the poem into a compelling, refined narrative while preserving all original themes.*

> There exists a distinct archetype of men who simply cannot conform—individuals driven by an incessant, internal restlessness. In their relentless pursuit of freedom, they break the hearts of loved ones as they wander the globe at will. Traversing vast fields, navigating open waters, and scaling mountain crests, they are bound by a persistent wanderlust that denies them tranquility.
> 
> Possessing strength, courage, and integrity, they might have achieved great distinction had they chosen a conventional path. However, perpetually dissatisfied with the status quo, they are compulsively drawn toward the unfamiliar. They often reassure themselves that discovering their true purpose would allow them to leave a profound legacy; yet, their frequent shifts in course result only in cumulative missteps.
> 
> In their brilliant but sporadic bursts of passion, they overlook a fundamental truth: lasting success belongs to those who persevere with quiet, steady discipline. Oblivious to the swift passage of time, they fail to notice the quiet departure of their youth and prime—until they are ultimately confronted by the stark, unyielding reality of their circumstances. 
> 
> Ultimately, they must confront the tragic realization of a life marked by unfulfilled potential and half-hearted endeavors. Life has played an ironic joke upon them, leaving them as permanent outsiders—restless spirits, born to wander, and fundamentally incapable of fitting in.

---

### Option 2: Professional & Analytical Style
*Best suited for psychological profiles, formal character studies, or professional presentations on human behavior.*

> Certain individuals possess an innate inability to conform to societal norms, driven by a chronic imperative to remain mobile. This ceaseless wanderlust often strains familial ties as they travel indiscriminately across diverse terrains and environments, unable to achieve personal stability.
> 
> While endowed with strength, bravery, and integrity—qualities that could yield significant success under disciplined conditions—these individuals are defined by a perpetual dissatisfaction with existing circumstances and a preference for novelty. They frequently operate under the assumption that finding an ideal environment will enable high achievement; however, their frequent strategic pivots consistently lead to compounding errors.
> 
> Furthermore, their reliance on intense, intermittent efforts causes them to underestimate the value of sustained, incremental progress, which traditionally yields long-term success. Consequently, they often remain unaware of their diminishing youth and capacity until forced to face the harsh reality of unachieved potential. 
> 
> In the final analysis, their lives reflect incomplete execution and missed opportunities. Defined by lifelong instability and an inability to integrate into established structures, they remain permanently unaligned with conventional success.

**The Tragedy of the Unsettled Soul**

Among us walk certain individuals consumed by an innate, almost inescapable urge to roam the world. Driven by an insatiable restlessness, they seem fundamentally incapable of tethering themselves to a single place, purpose, or person. While this spirit of adventure may appear romantic from a distance, its reality is often far darker. In their perpetual quest for the next horizon, these wanderers leave a quiet trail of devastation in their wake, repeatedly wounding the loved ones who care for them as they prove time and again that they simply cannot settle down.

What makes these men so tragic is that they are rarely lacking in capability. On the contrary, they often possess remarkable strength, daring courage, and the raw potential to achieve great success in whatever they turn their minds to. Yet, they are cursed by a chronic dissatisfaction with the status quo. For them, contentment feels like stagnation, and no present achievement can compete with the alluring promise of the unknown. They are perpetually seduced by novelty, mistaking the adrenaline of a new start for the fulfillment of a true calling.

This relentless desire for change ultimately becomes their undoing. By constantly pivoting toward new pursuits, they ruin their own momentum and condemn themselves to repeating the same foundational mistakes. True, enduring success is rarely built on erratic bursts of ambition; it demands the quiet, unglamorous discipline of steady persistence. Unwilling to endure the routine work required to bring any vision to full fruition, the wanderer confuses constant motion with actual progress, repeatedly abandoning half-built dreams to chase new ones.

Blinded by the thrill of the road, these men remain tragically indifferent to the relentless passage of time. They live as though youth were an infinite resource, convinced that there will always be another chance, another city, and another fresh start waiting around the corner. But time is an unyielding master. While they are busy pursuing distant illusions, their physical vigor wanes, the vigor of their youth slips away, and the prime opportunities of their lives quietly pass them by.

Ultimately, a lifelong refusal to commit leaves these wanderers entirely unanchored. Incapable of fitting into the society they so proudly resisted, they find themselves in the twilight of their lives not as triumphant free spirits, but as tragic failures. Stripped of their youthful energy and isolated from the bonds they fractured along the way, they are forced to confront a devastating truth. Too late, they realize that their grand journey was not a pursuit of greatness, but a flight from responsibility—and that in chasing everything, they built nothing at all.
outputs.L4:
**The Tragedy of the Restless Spirit: On Brilliance, Novelty, and Perseverance**

Among the varied afflictions of human character, few are as subtly destructive as the spirit of perpetual restlessness. There exists a class of men who, despite possessing talent, intellect, and lofty ambitions, seem utterly incapable of anchoring themselves to a single purpose or place. They view stability not as a foundation upon which to build a life, but as a cage from which they must continually escape. Driven by an insatiable hunger for the untried and the unknown, they repeatedly mistake mere motion for meaningful progress. Whenever a chosen path begins to demand the quiet monotony of routine, they abandon it, convinced that their true destiny lies just over the horizon in some unexamined enterprise.

The tragedy of these individuals lies not in a lack of exertion, but in the erratic, fitful nature of their energy. When captivated by a new concept or location, they throw themselves into the endeavor with feverish enthusiasm. For a brief period, they display a dazzling brilliance, outperforming those around them through sheer intensity. Yet, this burst of inspiration is inherently unsustainable. The moment the initial excitement fades—the moment the hard, unglamorous labor of maintenance begins—their focus wavers. The work that once inspired them suddenly feels like a burden, and their minds begin to wander toward the next bright promise, leaving a trail of half-finished endeavors in their wake.

By constantly resetting their trajectory, these men systematically destroy the very mechanism of long-term achievement: cumulative effort. Great undertakings—whether in art, business, or personal character—require time to mature. They demand that one endure the dry seasons when progress feels invisible. The restless man, however, constantly uproots his crops before they have time to take hold, forever seeking a more fertile soil that exists only in his imagination. Consequently, he forfeits his claims to mastery. He surrenders the profound rewards of deep investment in exchange for the shallow thrill of novel beginnings, constructing a life composed entirely of fragments.

As the years advance, the heavy toll of this behavior becomes painfully clear. The youth that once pardoned their fickleness slips away, leaving them to navigate a landscape of bitter regret. Looking back, they are forced to watch as contemporaries of far lesser natural gifts—men who simply possessed the fortitude to remain at their posts—reach the heights of success, security, and respect. The restless man is haunted by the realization that his life was not thwarted by bad luck or a hostile world, but by his own inability to endure. The novel experiences he so eagerly chased blur into a faint, meaningless haze, while the stability he so foolishly spurned reveals itself as the true treasure he lost.

Ultimately, the plight of the perpetually restless serves as a timeless moral lesson. Genius without discipline is merely a flashing meteor—spectacular for a brief moment, but leaving only darkness in its wake. True success, lasting fulfillment, and genuine strength of character are rarely the products of impulsive brilliance or the relentless pursuit of novelty. They belong instead to the quiet, unglamorous virtue of steady perseverance—the willingness to stay the course, endure the mundane, and finish what one has begun.

counterfactuals.prompt: Can you give me a classic poem that explores the tragic nature of restless wanderers—men who have great potential and courage, but constantly change course, never stick to one thing, and ultimately realize too late that they wasted their lives?
counterfactuals.output:
The poem that perfectly captures this exact theme—almost word for word—is **"The Men That Don't Fit In"** by **Robert W. Service** (published in 1907). 

Service was famous for writing about the rugged pioneers, prospectors, and vagabonds of the Yukon and the American West. In this poem, he paints a haunting and sympathetic portrait of men who possess immense talent, courage, and vision, but who are cursed with a restless spirit that forces them to constantly abandon their pursuits, leading to ultimate regret.

***

### The Men That Don't Fit In
*By Robert W. Service*

There’s a race of men that don’t fit in,
A race that can’t stay still;
So they break the hearts of kith and kin,
And they roam the world at will.
They range the field and they rove the flood,
And they climb the mountain’s crest;
Theirs is the curse of the gypsy blood,
And they never know repose or rest.

If they just went straight they might go far;
They are strong and brave and true;
But they set their face to the morning star,
And they cheer on the phantom crew.
The simple things that were good to know
They have spent their youth to learn;
They have pushing vigor and go,
And a vision bold and stern.

They start at sunrise with a song,
They are gold-mad or adventure-mad;
They carry the heavy loads along,
And they never look sad or glad.
They try the game for a little while,
They think they have found their place;
And then they turn with a weary smile,
And they drop right out of the race.

Some say God was tired when He made them;
Some say He forgot;
And some say He gave them a spark of fire,
And then He forgot the lot.
They are lightweights chasing a bubble,
They are fools for a word or a name;
They are men who are born for trouble,
And they play a losing game.

They fail, they fail, for they lack the grit
That carries the loser through;
They fall in the ditch, and they lie in it,
And they lie there dying too.
And the world goes by with a song and a laugh,
And a nod for the brave and bold;
And it leaves them there in the dirt and chaff,
To stiffen and freeze and grow cold.

He Harkens back to the old, old days,
When he was a boy at school;
And he sees the guy that he used to be,
A bright, ambitious fool.
He thinks of the work that he might have done,
And the places he might have filled;
He thinks of the battles he might have won,
And the house he might have built.

And he says, "If I had only stuck to it,
If I had only stayed;
If I had only grit to pull it through,
What a mark I might have made!"
So he dies in the ditch at last,
And the cold wind blows his hair;
And nobody knows and nobody cares,
For nobody's sitting there.

***

### Why this poem fits your prompt:
* **Great Potential & Courage:** Service notes that these men are "strong and brave and true," possessing "pushing vigor" and "a vision bold and stern." They aren't lazy; they are capable of incredible feats.
* **Constantly Changing Course:** "They try the game for a little while... And then they turn with a weary smile, / And they drop right out of the race." 
* **The Tragic Realization:** In the final stanzas, the wanderer reflects on "the battles he might have won" and utters the heartbreaking ultimate regret of the restless man: *"If I had only stuck to it... What a mark I might have made!"*
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

***

### The Men That Don't Fit In
**By Robert W. Service**

There's a race of men that don't fit in,
A race that can't stay still;
So they break the hearts of kith and kin,
And they roam the world at will.
They range the field and they rove the flood,
And they climb the mountain's crest;
Theirs is the curse of the gypsy blood,
And they don't know how to rest.

If they just went straight they might go far;
They are strong and brave and true;
But they're always tired of the things that are,
And they want the strange and new.
They say: "Could I find its black recess,
I'd mine the gold of a star?"
They quit the old for the chances less,
And they strike for the land afar.

Somebody marks the aforesaid spot,
He files the aforesaid claim;
He buys a mansion with all he's got,
And he plays the winning game.
While the other fellow who found the spot,
He's off again on the trail;
He isn't the sort to stay on the lot,
And he doesn't care for the kale.

He travels the world with a pack on his back,
Or a boat that he steers alone;
He follows the lure of the beaten track,
Or the call of the wild unknown.
He has suffered much, he has labored long,
He has fought with the frost and rain;
He has heard the siren's wilderness song,
And he's off on the trek again.

You say: "He is foolish, he doesn't care,
He's a failure, a good-for-naught."
And yet he's had what you didn't share,
He has fought the fight that he fought.
He has seen the beauty that shines afar,
He has loved the freedom and space;
He has hitched his wagon to a star,
And he's lost in the human race.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a traditional rhyming poem about a man who has "gypsy blood" and can never settle down, constantly chasing new things until he realizes he failed to make his mark in the end.
counterfactuals.output:
They said he bore a gypsy’s blood,  
A fire in his veins,  
He could not bear a steady roof,  
Or yield to gentle reins.  
The open road would whisper low,  
The wind was his delight,  
He packed his life in leather boots  
And vanished in the night.  

No cozy hearth could keep him warm,  
No soft love make him stay;  
He left a trail of broken vows  
Along his wandering way.  
For novelty was all he craved,  
The thrill of somewhere new,  
He drank the nectar of the wild  
And chased the morning dew.  

He sought the gloss of distant shores,  
The gleam of strange frontiers,  
He traded quiet, lasting peace  
For swift and gilded years.  
Each city was a fleeting stop,  
Each sunrise just a spark;  
He lived to run, he lived to roam,  
Unheeding of the dark.  

But time, the quiet hunter, came  
And stole his nimble stride,  
It laid a frost upon his brow  
And tamed his restless pride.  
His boots are thin, his knees are weak,  
The fire turned to rust,  
And all the shiny things he sought  
Have withered into dust.  

He sits alone beside the road  
And turns his head to see  
The long and winding path he walked,  
A hollow memory.  
He built no house of timber high,  
He sowed no fruitful field,  
No lasting work of heart or hand  
Did all his travels yield.  

His footprints in the shifting sand  
Were swallowed by the tide;  
He traded all the world could give  
To feed his foolish pride.  
A phantom on a lonely track,  
He leaves no shadow cast—  
A man who chased a thousand dreams,  
And made no mark at last.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

***

### **The Men That Don't Fit In**
*By Robert Service*

There's a race of men that don't fit in,  
A race that can't stay still;  
So they break the hearts of kith and kin,  
And they roam the world at will.  
They range the field and they rove the flood,  
And they climb the mountain's crest;  
Theirs is the curse of the gypsy blood,  
And they don't know how to rest.  

If they just went straight they might go far;  
They are strong and brave and true;  
But they're always tired of the things that are,  
And they want the strange and new.  
They say: "Could I find its black rim out,  
There's a wonderful place I think;"

And they lose on the blow-out's brink.  

They blow like spray on the hidden reef,  
They drive like foam on the sea;  
They find no rest and they know no grief,  
And they set their spirit free.  
They range the world and they play the game,

And they're forgotten before they're dead.
